objectives: Trace political science from the classical canon — Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Tocqueville.
Map the behavioral revolution — Easton, Almond + Verba, Dahl, Lijphart.
Survey the modern discipline — rational choice, new institutionalism, Acemoglu + Robinson.

slides.title: The classical canon: from Plato to Tocqueville
slides.body:
**Political science** = the systematic study of politics — power, authority, institutions, behavior, governance, conflict, cooperation. The discipline draws on a 2400-year tradition of political theory + a 20th-century behavioral + institutional empirical program.

**Plato (c. 428-348 BCE) — *Republic*** (c. 375 BCE). Plato proposes the ideal *kallipolis* — a city organized by reason, with philosopher-kings ruling a rigidly stratified order (guardians, auxiliaries, producers). The *tripartite soul* (reason, spirit, appetite) maps onto the tripartite polis. Justice = each part doing its proper work. Other dialogues — *Statesman*, *Laws*, *Gorgias* — refine the account. Plato's lasting questions: what is justice? who should rule? how do regimes degenerate (timocracy → oligarchy → democracy → tyranny)? Plato's hostility to democracy + his elitism remain foundational provocations.

**Aristotle (384-322 BCE) — *Politics*** (c. 350 BCE). Plato's student + the discipline's empirical founder. Aristotle + his Lyceum compiled 158 *constitutions* (only the *Constitution of the Athenians* survives) — comparative politics in embryo. Key contributions:
- **The polis is by nature** — humans are *zoon politikon* (political animals); the polis is logically + ethically prior to the household + individual.
- **The sixfold typology** of regimes: by *number who rule* (one, few, many) × *whose interest* (common, ruling part's). Monarchy / tyranny; aristocracy / oligarchy; polity / democracy. The first of each pair pursues the common good; the second the rulers' interest.
- **The polity (mixed regime)** as the best practicable — combining oligarchic + democratic elements, anchored in a substantial middle class.
- **Distributive vs corrective justice**; **practical wisdom (*phronesis*)**; the polis aims at *eudaimonia* (flourishing).
Aristotle founded comparative politics + political philosophy + remains an essential interlocutor.

**Niccolò Machiavelli (1469-1527) — *The Prince*** (1513; published posthumously 1532) + ***Discourses on Livy*** (1517). The Florentine secretary's two faces:
- ***The Prince***: how a *new* prince acquires + maintains power. Realism over moralism. *Virtù* (calculated capacity) vs *Fortuna* (chance). The ends-means logic — 'it is better to be feared than loved if one cannot be both'. Reading him as merely cynical misses the republican commitments of the *Discourses*.
- ***Discourses***: defends mixed republics on Roman model; popular tumults + class conflict as engines of liberty + civic virtue.
Machiavelli inaugurated *political realism* + the autonomous study of power. The adjective 'Machiavellian' is much narrower than the man.

**Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679) — *Leviathan*** (1651). Written amid the English Civil War. The *state of nature* is a war 'of every man against every man'; life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. To escape, individuals contract together to authorize a sovereign — the Leviathan — with absolute power to keep the peace. Hobbes's geometric materialism + methodological individualism + social-contract framing founded modern political theory. He is sometimes read as the founder of liberalism (the contract grounds authority in individual consent) + sometimes as the patron of absolutism.

**John Locke (1632-1704) — *Two Treatises of Government*** (1689). Reply to Robert Filmer's patriarchalism + a Whig defense of the Glorious Revolution.
- **State of nature** is governed by natural law + reason; persons have natural rights to *life, liberty, property* (the labor theory of property: mix labor with nature → ownership).
- **Government by consent**, with limited powers, separation of legislative + executive, + a right to *revolution* if rulers violate the trust.
- Liberal constitutionalism's foundational text. Influenced the American Founders (Jefferson, Madison) + the Declaration of Independence.

**Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712-1778) — *The Social Contract*** (1762) + ***Discourse on Inequality*** (1755). 'Man is born free, but everywhere he is in chains.' Civil society *corrupts* natural goodness; only a republic grounded in the **general will** can reconcile freedom + authority. The general will is *not* the will of all (sum of individual wills) but the will aimed at the common good. Rousseau is the philosophical fountainhead of democratic + republican + (more controversially, per Berlin + Talmon) totalitarian-democratic traditions. Hugely influential on the French Revolution + on Kant + Hegel.

**Alexis de Tocqueville (1805-1859) — *Democracy in America*** (vol. 1 1835; vol. 2 1840). A Norman aristocrat's nine-month 1831 tour of the U.S. produced the discipline's first great empirical-comparative-historical study of democracy. Themes:
- *Equality of conditions* is the master fact of modernity; democracy is inevitable but ambiguous.
- **Tyranny of the majority** — soft despotism + conformity pressure as democracy's pathologies.
- **Civil society + voluntary associations** as the antidote — Americans 'are forever forming associations'.
- **Mores (*moeurs*)** + religion + the township + the jury as schools of self-government.
- ***The Old Regime and the Revolution*** (1856) — explained the French Revolution through long-run administrative centralization.
Tocqueville inaugurated comparative-historical political sociology + remains the canonical analyst of democratic culture.

slides.title: The behavioral revolution: Easton, Almond, Verba, Dahl, Lijphart
slides.body:
By 1950, U.S. political science was institutionalized but theoretically thin — historical-descriptive accounts of formal institutions. The **behavioral revolution** (c. 1945-1970) refounded the discipline on systematic empirical observation + quantitative method + general theory.

**David Easton (1917-2014) — political systems framework**. *The Political System* (1953); *A Framework for Political Analysis* (1965); *A Systems Analysis of Political Life* (1965). Easton defined politics as 'the authoritative allocation of values for a society'. The political system is a *black box* converting *inputs* (demands + support from the environment) into *outputs* (authoritative decisions + actions) with *feedback*. Easton's *systems* framing gave the discipline a unifying vocabulary + made it possible to compare polities + study political development. Critics (Almond, Lasswell) noted the framework was descriptive rather than predictive; later work refined it.

**Gabriel Almond (1911-2002) + Sidney Verba (1932-2019) — *The Civic Culture*** (1963). The discipline's first great five-nation cross-national survey (U.S., U.K., West Germany, Italy, Mexico, c. 1959-1960). Distinguished three political-culture types:
- **Parochial** — citizens have little awareness of the national political system.
- **Subject** — citizens are aware of the system as objects of its outputs but not as participants.
- **Participant** — citizens see themselves as active participants.
A *civic culture* mixes participant + subject + parochial orientations — civic competence + deference + community — + provides the cultural underpinning of stable democracy. Almond + Verba's framework + survey-based comparison founded modern political culture research + comparative politics as a quantitative subfield. Critique: the *democratic congruence* thesis was too tightly tied to Anglo-American norms (Inglehart's *World Values Survey* + later work generalized).

**Robert Dahl (1915-2014) — pluralism + polyarchy**. Yale's intellectual giant; led the post-war behavioral program.
- ***A Preface to Democratic Theory*** (1956): classical (Madisonian + populistic) vs procedural democracy; the practical conditions of democratic rule.
- ***Who Governs?*** (1961): a study of power in New Haven; influence is *plural* + *issue-specific* rather than monolithic (Floyd Hunter's elite theory + C. Wright Mills's *Power Elite* notwithstanding). Founded **pluralism** as the dominant U.S. account of democratic politics.
- ***Polyarchy*** (1971): no actual democracy meets the philosophical ideal; usable concept = **polyarchy** with two dimensions — *contestation* (free competition for power) + *inclusiveness* (broad participation). Eight institutional conditions — elected officials, free + fair elections, inclusive suffrage, right to run for office, freedom of expression, alternative information, associational autonomy, accountability. Polyarchy is now the working definition behind major democracy indices (V-Dem, Freedom House, Polity).
- ***On Democracy*** (1998); ***How Democratic is the American Constitution?*** (2001).
Dahl's pluralism + polyarchy frame contemporary democratic theory + empirical democratization research.

**Arend Lijphart (b. 1936) — consensus vs majoritarian democracy**. Dutch-American comparativist.
- ***The Politics of Accommodation*** (1968): how deeply divided societies (Netherlands) maintain stability through elite cooperation + power-sharing — *consociationalism* (grand coalitions, mutual veto, proportionality, segmental autonomy).
- ***Democracies*** (1984) + ***Patterns of Democracy*** (1999, 2012): coded ~36 democracies on ten institutional dimensions; found two clusters — **majoritarian (Westminster) democracies** (UK, NZ, post-1958 France) concentrate power; **consensus democracies** (Switzerland, Belgium, Netherlands, Germany) disperse it across coalitions, parliaments, federalism, judicial review. Consensus democracies show somewhat better policy + welfare outcomes + roughly equivalent economic performance.
Lijphart's empirical typology shaped institutional-design debates worldwide. Discussion + critique: Powell *Elections as Instruments of Democracy* (2000); Andeweg + Powell critiques.

**Related landmark behavioral works**:
- **Anthony Downs *An Economic Theory of Democracy*** (1957) — rational-choice spatial model of voting + parties (deep in lesson 4 + lesson 7).
- **William Riker *The Theory of Political Coalitions*** (1962) — minimum winning coalitions.
- **Mancur Olson *The Logic of Collective Action*** (1965) — public-goods + group-size logic (deep in lesson 7).
- **Campbell, Converse, Miller, Stokes *The American Voter*** (1960) — Michigan model of partisanship + voting (deep in lesson 6).
- **Almond + Powell *Comparative Politics: A Developmental Approach*** (1966); Almond + Coleman *The Politics of the Developing Areas* (1960).
- **Karl Deutsch *The Nerves of Government*** (1963) — cybernetics in politics.

The behavioral revolution made political science a rigorously empirical discipline. Its excesses (atheoretical data-grubbing; American-centric assumptions; neglect of power inequalities + history) prompted the **post-behavioral** reaction (Easton's APSA Presidential Address 1969) + the **historical institutionalist** + **rational choice** turns that organize the next slide.

slides.title: Modern political science: rational choice, institutionalism, and the development turn
slides.body:
From the 1970s onward, political science became theoretically pluralistic — three big approaches dominate, alongside enduring normative + interpretive work.

**Rational choice theory** + **positive political theory**. Imported microeconomic methods.
- **Anthony Downs** *An Economic Theory of Democracy* (1957) — the *median voter theorem* + the *Downsian spatial model*. Parties converge to the median in one-dimensional, two-party plurality systems with sincere voting.
- **William Riker** *The Theory of Political Coalitions* (1962); *Liberalism Against Populism* (1982) — Arrow's theorem (lesson 4) means democracy cannot be *populist* (no coherent 'will of the people'); it is *liberal* (a mechanism for removing bad rulers).
- **Kenneth Arrow** *Social Choice and Individual Values* (1951) — the impossibility theorem (lesson 4).
- **Allan Gibbard 1973** + **Mark Satterthwaite 1975** — strategic-voting impossibility (lesson 4).
- **Kenneth Shepsle + Barry Weingast** — *structure-induced equilibrium* (1979); how legislative institutions tame multidimensional chaos.
- **Gary Cox + Mathew McCubbins** — party government + the cartel theory of legislative organization.
- **Bruce Bueno de Mesquita + Alastair Smith** *The Logic of Political Survival* (2003); *The Dictator's Handbook* (2011) — selectorate theory.
Rational choice is *the* analytic engine of modern American politics + IR (game-theoretic + bargaining models) + comparative political economy.

**New institutionalism** — the *return* of institutions in three flavors (Hall + Taylor 1996, *Political Studies*):
- **Rational-choice institutionalism** — institutions as equilibrium-selection devices; Shepsle, Weingast, North, Tsebelis (*Veto Players* 2002).
- **Historical institutionalism** — *Structuring Politics* (Steinmo, Thelen, Longstreth 1992); *Policy Feedback* (Skocpol; Pierson *Politics in Time* 2004); **path dependence** + **critical junctures** + **policy feedback** (cross-ref Mahoney + Acemoglu-Robinson below). Thelen *How Institutions Evolve* (2004); Capoccia + Kelemen critical-junctures framework.
- **Sociological institutionalism** — institutions as taken-for-granted scripts + legitimacy; March + Olsen *Rediscovering Institutions* (1989); world-society / world-culture school (Meyer, Boli, Thomas, Ramirez).

**Comparative political development + the state**:
- **Theda Skocpol** *States and Social Revolutions* (1979) — structural comparative analysis of France, Russia, China; *Bringing the State Back In* (Evans + Rueschemeyer + Skocpol 1985) — repudiated society-centric pluralism.
- **Charles Tilly** *The Formation of National States in Western Europe* (1975); *Coercion, Capital, and European States* (1990) — 'war made the state, and the state made war'. The bargain — taxation for representation — drove European state-building (cross-ref comparative politics, lesson 3).
- **Samuel Huntington** *Political Order in Changing Societies* (1968) — institutionalization vs participation; *The Third Wave* (1991) — democratization since 1974.
- **Guillermo O'Donnell + Philippe Schmitter** *Transitions from Authoritarian Rule* (1986) — the transitions paradigm.

**Daron Acemoglu + James Robinson — *Why Nations Fail*** (2012); *Economic Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy* (2006); *The Narrow Corridor* (2019). Acemoglu's 2024 Economics Nobel (with Johnson + Robinson). Central thesis:
- **Inclusive institutions** (broadly distributed political + economic rights; secure property; investment in human capital; constraints on rulers) generate growth + welfare.
- **Extractive institutions** (narrow elite control; insecure property for non-elites; rent-extraction) generate stagnation.
- *Critical junctures* (Black Death; Atlantic trade; colonial encounters) interact with prior institutions to produce divergent paths — explaining the long-run wealth gap between, e.g., the U.S. + Mexico; North + South Korea.
Acemoglu + Robinson are now the dominant frame for political-economy + comparative-development questions (cross-ref lessons 3 + 7).

**Other modern lineages**:
- **James Mahoney** *Colonialism and Postcolonial Development* (2010); Mahoney + Thelen *Explaining Institutional Change* (2010); *path dependence* + *reactive sequences*.
- **Francis Fukuyama** *The End of History and the Last Man* (1992); *The Origins of Political Order* (2011) + *Political Order and Political Decay* (2014); state + rule of law + accountability as the three pillars.
- **Adam Przeworski** *Democracy and the Market* (1991); *Democracy and Development* (2000) — democracy survives above ~$6000-12000 per-capita income.
- **Steven Levitsky + Lucan Way** *Competitive Authoritarianism* (2010); *Revolution and Dictatorship* (2022) — hybrid regimes (lesson 3).
- **Pippa Norris** electoral integrity + cultural backlash (lessons 4 + 8).

**The discipline today** is organized around four main subfields — political theory, comparative politics, international relations, American politics — plus a methods subfield + interdisciplinary frontiers (political economy, political behavior, computational + experimental political science). The remaining lessons develop each: theory (lesson 2), comparative (lesson 3), electoral systems + voting (lesson 4), international relations (lesson 5), American politics (lesson 6), political economy (lesson 7), the computational + AI frontier (lesson 8).

A persistent tension: the discipline aspires to be *scientific* + *predictive* yet studies a domain — politics — saturated with power, contestation, value disagreement, + historical contingency. Each tradition negotiates this tension differently.

question.question: Reason through Aristotle's sixfold regime typology + its modern uses
question.goal: Show how Aristotle's *Politics* (c. 350 BCE) classified regimes + why political scientists still use the framework.

steps.prompt: What two variables did Aristotle use to classify regimes?

acceptedAnswers: number who rule (one, few, many) and whose interest is pursued (common good vs ruling part's interest)

steps.reveal: Aristotle crossed (a) the **number who rule** — one, few, many — with (b) **whose interest is pursued** — the common good of the polis, or the ruling part's interest. The 2 × 3 grid yields six pure types: monarchy / tyranny; aristocracy / oligarchy; polity / democracy. The first of each pair pursues the common good; the second is its corrupted form.

steps.prompt: Which regime did Aristotle consider best in practice + why?

acceptedAnswers: polity, a mixed regime anchored in a large middle class that balances oligarchic and democratic tendencies

steps.reveal: Aristotle judged the **polity** — a mixed regime combining oligarchic + democratic elements — to be the best *practicable* regime. A large + secure **middle class** moderates the extremes of rich + poor + sustains stability + civic virtue. Aristotle's anti-extremist + class-balanced ideal echoes through Polybius, Cicero, Machiavelli's *Discourses*, Madison's *Federalist 10*, + modern moderate-democracy theory.

steps.prompt: How do modern indices map onto Aristotle's typology?

acceptedAnswers: modern indices like polity v-dem freedom house track Aristotle's interest-of-rulers dimension via inclusiveness and contestation; the number-of-rulers dimension matters less directly

hints: Polity, V-Dem, Freedom House, Dahl's polyarchy.
steps.reveal: Modern indices — Polity, V-Dem, Freedom House, Dahl's polyarchy (1971) — operationalize Aristotle's *whose-interest* dimension via *contestation* + *inclusiveness*. The *number-of-rulers* dimension matters less directly (we rarely have monarchies; oligarchy + democracy blur). V-Dem's many indicators + the *liberal*, *electoral*, *participatory*, *deliberative*, *egalitarian* democracy components substantially refine the Aristotelian classification. The conceptual scaffolding remains useful.

steps.prompt: What is the framework's biggest limitation today?

acceptedAnswers: binary good or corrupt distinction misses hybrid regimes and slow processes of democratic backsliding; modern scholarship needs continuous and multidimensional measures

steps.reveal: The biggest limit: Aristotle's *binary* good/corrupt distinction misses **hybrid regimes** (competitive authoritarianism — Levitsky + Way 2010; electoral autocracy — V-Dem) + the *processes* of democratic backsliding (Bermeo 2016; Levitsky + Ziblatt 2018). Modern political science prefers continuous + multidimensional measures (V-Dem; Polity5; the Economist Intelligence Unit Democracy Index). Aristotle's framework supplies scaffolding + intuitions; the empirical work refines them.

question.question: Why was Tocqueville's *Democracy in America* (1835-1840) foundational for political science?
options: Tocqueville (1805-1859), an aristocratic French observer, produced after a nine-month 1831 U.S. tour the discipline's first great empirical-comparative-historical study of democracy. He treated *equality of conditions* as modernity's master fact + democracy as inevitable but ambiguous; identified the *tyranny of the majority* + soft despotism + conformity as democracy's pathologies; named *civil society + voluntary associations + mores + religion + the township + the jury* as schools of self-government; + showed comparatively (with France) how administrative centralization shapes regime fates (*The Old Regime and the Revolution* 1856). His method — careful comparison + thick observation + structural reasoning — inaugurated comparative-historical political sociology + comparative politics. He anticipated Almond + Verba on civic culture, Putnam on social capital, + Dahl on pluralism. His warnings about democratic conformity + soft despotism resonate in current debates over democratic backsliding + the algorithmic public sphere.
question.explanation: Tocqueville's *Democracy in America* (1835-1840) inaugurated comparative-historical political analysis — equality of conditions; tyranny of the majority; civil society + associations + mores as schools of self-government. He anticipated Almond + Verba civic culture, Putnam social capital, Dahl pluralism, + remains essential for contemporary democratic-backsliding + algorithmic-public-sphere debates.

hints: What did he see in America?
slides.workedSolution: Tocqueville's *Democracy in America* (1835-1840) — equality of conditions, tyranny of the majority, civil society + voluntary associations as schools of self-government — inaugurated comparative-historical political sociology + anticipated Almond-Verba civic culture, Putnam social capital, Dahl pluralism. Still essential for backsliding + algorithmic-public-sphere debates.

question.question: Translating a classical question into a modern research design
question.prompt: A graduate student wants to test Tocqueville's claim that *voluntary associations* sustain democratic stability. Drawing explicitly on (a) Almond + Verba's *Civic Culture* (1963) cross-national survey; (b) Dahl's polyarchy framework (1971); (c) Lijphart's consensus-vs-majoritarian typology (1999); + (d) Acemoglu + Robinson's institutions argument (*Why Nations Fail* 2012), write a paragraph (≤200 words) outlining a research design. Identify three concrete empirical questions + one specific dataset (V-Dem, ANES, WVS, ESS) you would use.

question.question: Lijphart's *Patterns of Democracy* codes a country on $d = 10$ institutional dimensions; consensus democracies score on the consensual end of each, majoritarian on the majoritarian end. If a country scores $+1$ on $7$ dimensions and $-1$ on $3$ dimensions (consensus = $+1$, majoritarian = $-1$), compute the country's mean dimension score to one decimal place.
question.hint: $(7 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot (-1)) / 10 = 4 / 10 = 0.4$. Lijphart's index summarizes ten institutional features into two composite dimensions (executives-parties + federal-unitary). Positive scores indicate consensus democracy (Switzerland, Belgium, Netherlands); negative indicate majoritarian (UK, NZ pre-1996). Mean $\approx 0.4$ would place a country on the consensus side.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain what makes political science a distinct discipline by naming (a) one core insight from each of Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, + Tocqueville; (b) what the behavioral revolution added (name Easton + Almond + Verba + Dahl + Lijphart); + (c) what Acemoglu + Robinson + new institutionalism contribute.
question.rubric: Mentions: Plato (*Republic* c. 375 BCE — justice + philosopher-kings + regime degeneration); Aristotle (*Politics* — empirical comparison + sixfold typology + mixed-regime polity); Machiavelli (*The Prince* 1513 + *Discourses* 1517 — autonomous study of power + virtù vs fortuna); Hobbes (*Leviathan* 1651 — social contract + sovereignty + state-of-nature individualism); Locke (*Two Treatises* 1689 — natural rights + consent + right of revolution); Rousseau (*Social Contract* 1762 — general will + republican democracy); Tocqueville (*Democracy in America* 1835-1840 — equality of conditions + civil society + tyranny of the majority + comparative-historical method). Behavioral revolution: Easton political systems; Almond + Verba *Civic Culture* (1963) cross-national survey; Dahl polyarchy (1971); Lijphart consensus vs majoritarian (1999). Modern: rational choice (Downs Riker Arrow); new institutionalism (Hall + Taylor 1996); Acemoglu + Robinson *Why Nations Fail* (2012) inclusive vs extractive institutions. Concludes that the discipline unifies normative + structural + behavioral + institutional lenses on power + governance.
